h1: Someone Else Controls Your Restaurant's Google Listing: How to Take It Back
metaTitle: How to Claim Your Restaurant's Google Listing
metaDescription: Someone else controls your restaurant's Google listing? Here is how to claim your restaurant on Google, request access, verify, and take back control.

directAnswer: To claim your restaurant on Google when someone else controls the listing, search your business on Google and click "Own this business?", or go to business.google.com/add and select your restaurant. If Google says it is already managed, click Request access and fill out the short form with your name, your role, and a contact number. The current owner has about three to seven days to approve or deny; if they do not respond, Google usually lets you claim it yourself and verify by video or postcard. If the request is denied, verify your way in by video, because you can prove you operate the address.

intro:
You go to update your holiday hours on Google, or reply to a review, and you hit a wall. Google says the profile is "already managed by someone else," or every edit you try simply will not save. Somewhere out there, a person or company you may not even remember is holding the keys to how your restaurant shows up online.

That listing is your Google Business Profile, the free box with your name, hours, photos, and reviews that appears on Google and drops the red pin on Google Maps. When someone else controls it, they can change your hours, your phone number, even your address, and you cannot. The good news: Google has a built-in process to take it back, and you do not need to be technical to use it.

This guide walks you through it click by click: how these lock-outs happen, how to find out who has control, how to request access, what the current holder sees on their end, and exactly what to do if they say no.

sections.h2: What does it mean when someone else controls your listing?
sections.html:
First, the one term that matters. Your Google Business Profile is the free listing Google gives every real business. It is the panel with your name, hours, photos, phone number, and reviews that appears when someone searches for you, plus the red pin on Google Maps. When people say a restaurant "is on Google," this is what they mean.

Every profile has an owner, the account with full control, and it can also have managers, accounts allowed to make edits. The owner can change your name, address, hours, and phone, add or remove other people, and even mark the place as closed. A profile is verified once someone has proven to Google that they run the business. Only a verified profile can be edited, and only the owner account can hand control to someone else.

So when Google tells you the profile is "already managed" or your edits will not stick, it means another Google account is the verified owner. That could be harmless (an old account of yours) or a real problem (a former partner or a vendor who will not let go). Either way, the fix is the same process, and it is free.

sections.h2: How did someone else end up with your restaurant's listing?
sections.html:
Knowing how you got locked out helps you pick the right path back. Here are the common ways it happens to Miami restaurants.

  • A former owner or business partner. You bought the restaurant, or a partner left, and the Google profile stayed under their personal account. Very common when a place changes hands.
  • A marketing agency or web company. Whoever built your website or ran your ads a few years ago created the profile under their own account "to help," and never transferred it. When you part ways, they still hold it.
  • An employee's personal Gmail. A manager or family member set it up on their own account, then left. The login walked out the door with them.
  • Google created it automatically. Google generates unclaimed listings from public data (phone directories, delivery apps, city records). No one owns it yet, which actually makes it easier to claim.
  • A customer or a delivery app added it. Someone checked in, or a delivery app listed you, and a basic profile appeared.
  • A "verification service" scam. A caller or emailer offered to "verify" or "fix" your Google listing, you gave them access, and now a stranger controls it. Google never charges for this, so treat those calls as a warning sign.

sections.h2: How do you find out who controls it?
sections.html:
Start by seeing exactly what Google shows. You do not need any special tool, just a web browser and the Google account you want to use for the restaurant going forward. If you do not have a dedicated business Google account yet, make one first, because whoever holds that account will control the listing.

  1. Open a web browser and go to google.com.
  2. Search your exact restaurant name plus your city, like Casa Lola Little Havana.
  3. Look at the panel that appears on the right on a computer, or near the top on a phone. Scroll to the bottom of it.
  4. Look for a small link that says Own this business? or Claim this business. If you see it, the profile is unclaimed or claimable, and you are in luck. Jump to the next section.
  5. If instead you click through and Google says the profile is already verified or managed by someone else, another account owns it. That is the request access path, a couple of sections down.

Google will not tell you the full email of the current owner, for privacy, but when you start a request it usually shows a masked hint, like c****@gmail.com. That hint alone often tells you whether it is your own old account, a former partner, or an agency.

sections.h2: How do you claim a listing nobody has verified yet?
sections.html:
If you saw Own this business? or Claim this business, no one has verified the profile, so you can take it directly. This is the simplest case.

  1. Make sure you are signed in with the business Google account. Check the colored circle in the top right corner of the browser. If it is the wrong account, click it and switch.
  2. On the search panel, click Claim this business or Own this business?. You can also go straight to business.google.com, click Manage now, and search your name there.
  3. Confirm the details Google shows are yours, and follow the prompts.
  4. Google will ask you to verify, which means prove you run the place. Skip ahead to the verification section for exactly what that involves.

Once you verify, the profile is fully yours and you can fix the hours, photos, and everything else. If it was never claimed by anyone, you are done after verifying, with no access request needed.

sections.h2: How do you request access when it says already managed?
sections.html:
This is the path when another account is the verified owner. You cannot just take it. Google makes you ask the current holder, then steps in if they do not cooperate. Here is the request, step by step.

  1. In your browser, signed in with your business account, go to business.google.com/add (or click Own this business? on the search panel).
  2. Type your restaurant name and address and select it from the list.
  3. You will see a message like "Someone else may manage this Business Profile." Click Request access (sometimes shown as Request admin rights or Get access).
  4. Fill out the short form. Google typically asks for the level of access you want (choose Owner if you want full control, or Manager for editing only), your relationship to the business (for example, owner), and your name and contact phone number.
  5. Click Submit. Google sends you a confirmation email with your request details and next steps.

Keep your reason short and honest, something like "I am the current owner of this restaurant and need to manage the listing." That message goes to the person who holds the profile, so keep it professional.

sections.h2: What does the current owner see, and how long do you wait?
sections.html:
The moment you submit, Google emails the current owner and asks them to approve or deny you. Here is what to expect while you wait.

  • They get an email right away. It names your request and gives them a link to grant or refuse access.
  • They have a few days to answer. Google gives the current owner roughly three to seven days to respond. During that window you simply wait, and you cannot edit the profile yet.
  • If they approve, control (or access) transfers to your account and you get an email. Done.
  • If they ignore the request, and the days pass with no answer, Google usually lets you claim the profile yourself. Go back to the same request screen and look for an option to claim or verify. You then prove ownership through verification, covered next.
  • If they deny it, you get an email saying so. That is not the end of the road. See the denial section below.

Check the email you used for the request, including your spam folder, because Google's follow-up is how you move forward once the waiting period ends.

sections.h2: How do you verify that the restaurant is really yours?
sections.html:
Whether you are claiming an unowned listing or taking over after a no-response, Google makes you verify, which just means proving you run a real business at this address. Google decides which methods you get, so you cannot always choose. For restaurants in 2026, video is by far the most common.

  • Video recording (most common for restaurants). You record one short, continuous video, usually under two minutes, on your phone inside the verification screen. Show three things: where you are (the street, your outdoor sign, the building number), that it is your business (your signage, menu, and interior), and that you run it (unlock the front door, step into a staff-only area, or open the register). Film in daylight, in one take, and do not stop recording. Google usually reviews it within about five business days.
  • Postcard. Google mails a card with a code to your address, which takes about five to fourteen days. When it arrives, sign in and type in the code.
  • Phone or email. For some businesses Google sends a code by text, call, or email that you type in within minutes. Restaurants are offered this less often now.

A little care pays off. A clear video that shows your name on the sign and proof you have keys to the place passes far more often than a rushed, dark, or edited one.

sections.h2: What if your request is denied?
sections.html:
A denial feels like a dead end, but you usually still have moves. This is common when a former agency or partner refuses, or when Google's automatic check is cautious. Work through these in order.

  1. Reach out to the holder directly first. If you know the former partner, manager, or agency, a simple call asking them to approve the request or add you as an owner is the fastest fix. Many denials are just someone who never opened the email.
  2. Submit the request again with more detail. Re-run the request and clearly state that you are the current owner. Sometimes a second, clearer request gets approved.
  3. Verify your way in. After a denial or a stalled request, Google often gives you the option to claim and verify the profile yourself by video or postcard. Because you can physically prove you operate the address, this is your strongest card, since a distant former vendor cannot stand at your front door.
  4. Use Google's own help channels. From your Google Business Profile, look for Help or Contact us to reach support, explain that you are the rightful owner, and ask them to review the ownership conflict.

If your restaurant also disappeared from search or the map during all this, that is a separate but related issue. Our step-by-step guide on why your restaurant is not showing up on Google Maps and how to fix it walks through suspensions, duplicates, and verification snags.

faqs.q: How do I claim my restaurant on Google if someone else already owns the listing?
faqs.a: Search your restaurant on Google and click "Own this business?", or go to business.google.com/add and select your restaurant. If Google says it is already managed, click Request access and fill out the short form with the level of access you want, your relationship to the business, and your contact number. Google emails the current owner, who has about three to seven days to approve or deny. If they do not respond, Google usually lets you claim the profile yourself and verify ownership, most often with a short video.

faqs.q: How long does the current owner have to respond to my access request?
faqs.a: Google gives the current owner roughly three to seven days to respond to an access request. During that time you cannot edit the profile and simply wait. If the owner approves, access transfers to you. If they ignore the request past the waiting period, Google usually gives you the option to claim the profile yourself and verify it, so a no-response does not block you forever.

faqs.q: What happens if the current owner denies or ignores my request?
faqs.a: If they ignore it, Google usually lets you claim the listing yourself once the three to seven day window passes, then verify by video or postcard. If they actively deny it, you still have options: contact the holder directly to ask them to approve or add you, submit a clearer request again, or verify your way in by recording a video at the restaurant. Because you can physically prove you operate the address, verification is usually your strongest path.

faqs.q: A marketing company set up my Google listing and will not give it back. What can I do?
faqs.a: First, ask them directly to add you as an owner or approve your access request, since that is the fastest fix and many holdouts simply never opened the email. If they refuse, submit an access request at business.google.com/add and, when it stalls or is denied, use the option to claim and verify the profile yourself by video. You can prove you run the restaurant from the front door, which a former vendor cannot, and that is often what settles the conflict. Google never requires you to pay a third party to keep your free listing online.

faqs.q: Can I just create a new listing instead of dealing with the old one?
faqs.a: No, avoid this. Creating a second listing gives you a duplicate that competes with the original, splits your reviews, and can get both profiles hidden or suspended. Google's system is built around one verified profile per real location. Always claim or request access to the existing listing rather than starting a new one, even when the old one is frustrating to reach.

faqs.q: How do I remove a former owner or partner from my Google Business Profile?
faqs.a: You must first be the primary owner of the profile. Once you have control, sign in at business.google.com, open your profile, go to the businesses or the people and access section, find the person, and remove them. If a former owner still holds the primary ownership and will not release it, you cannot remove them directly. You request access or an ownership transfer instead, and verify the business if they do not respond.

faqs.q: What does the video verification for a restaurant need to show?
faqs.a: Record one short, continuous video (usually under two minutes) on your phone that proves three things: where you are (the street, your outdoor sign, the building number), that it is your business (your signage, menu, and interior), and that you run it (unlocking the door, entering a staff-only area, or opening the register). Film in daylight, in a single take, and do not stop recording. Google typically reviews restaurant videos within about five business days.

faqs.q: Is it free to claim or recover my restaurant's Google listing?
faqs.a: Yes. Claiming, requesting access to, verifying, and managing a Google Business Profile is completely free. Google makes its money from ads, not from your basic listing. If someone calls or emails offering to "verify" or "release" your listing for a fee, treat it as a red flag, because Google does not charge for this. You may choose to pay an agency to handle the process for you, but the listing itself costs nothing.
